task1.title: Internet access
task1.prompt: The graph shows the percentage of households with internet access in three countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph compares the proportion of households with internet access in Canada, Brazil and India between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, access rose steadily in all three countries over the period, although Canada remained the most connected nation throughout, while India, despite starting from the lowest base, recorded the most dramatic growth in the final decade.

In 2000, just over two-fifths of Canadian households (42%) were online, compared with 18% in Brazil and a mere 9% in India. Over the following ten years, the Canadian figure climbed to 66%, whereas Brazil saw its share more than double to 47%. India, by contrast, progressed relatively slowly, reaching only 24% by 2010.

From 2010 onwards, the gap between the three countries narrowed considerably. Canada continued its upward trend to finish at 82% in 2020, and Brazil rose at a similar pace to 72%. Meanwhile, the proportion of connected homes in India accelerated sharply, more than doubling in ten years to reach 55% by the end of the period, although it still lagged some way behind the other two countries.

task1.title: International tourist arrivals in three cities
task1.prompt: The graph below shows the number of international tourists (in millions) who visited three cities between 2004 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The line graph illustrates how many international visitors, in millions, travelled to Lisbon, Prague and Vienna over a twenty-year period from 2004 to 2024.

Overall, all three cities attracted more foreign tourists by the end of the period, despite a dramatic collapse in 2020. The most striking feature is the rapid rise of Lisbon, which began as the least visited city but finished well ahead of the other two.

In 2004, Prague was the most popular destination with 4.2 million arrivals, followed by Vienna with 3.5 million, while Lisbon received only 2.1 million. Over the next twelve years, Prague and Vienna grew steadily, reaching 5.6 and 4.7 million respectively in 2016. Lisbon, however, expanded far more quickly, more than doubling to 4.8 million and drawing level with Vienna.

In 2020, visitor numbers plummeted in every city to between 1.2 and 1.4 million. The recovery that followed was uneven: by 2024 Lisbon had surged to a peak of 5.9 million, whereas Prague (5.3 million) had not quite regained its earlier level and Vienna climbed only slightly above it, to 4.9 million.

task1.title: Weekly exercise by age and gender
task1.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of men and women in one country who did at least 150 minutes of exercise per week in 2022, by age group. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares the proportions of men and women in one country who exercised for at least 150 minutes a week in 2022, across six age groups.

Overall, participation in regular exercise declined steadily with age for both sexes. Men were more active than women in every age bracket, although the difference was most noticeable among the youngest and oldest adults.

Among 16- to 24-year-olds, almost three-quarters of men (74%) met the weekly target, compared with 63% of women, a gap of eleven percentage points. For men, the figure then fell consistently, to 61% in the 35–44 group and 55% among those aged 45 to 54. The decrease for women over the same ages was much more gradual, from 60% to 54%, which meant that the two sexes were almost level in middle age.

In the older age groups, the downward trend continued. Just under half of men aged 55 to 64 exercised sufficiently, compared with 47% of women. The lowest rates were recorded among people aged 65 and over, where only 38% of men and fewer than a third of women (31%) reached the recommended level.

task1.title: Household spending, 1980 and 2020
task1.prompt: The pie charts below show how the average household in one country spent its income in 1980 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The two pie charts illustrate the proportion of income that an average household in one country allocated to six categories of expenditure in 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the pattern of spending changed considerably over the forty years. Whereas food was the largest single expense in 1980, housing had become by far the biggest outgoing by 2020, and leisure also grew in importance.

In 1980, almost a third of household income (32%) was spent on food, while housing accounted for just over a fifth (21%). Transport took 14% of the budget, clothing 11% and leisure a modest 9%. The remaining 13% went on other items.

By 2020, the share devoted to housing had risen sharply to 34%, making it more than twice as large as the proportion spent on food, which had almost halved to 17%. Similarly, spending on clothing fell from 11% to only 5%. In contrast, leisure activities absorbed a significantly larger share, at 16%, while the figures for transport and other expenses remained virtually unchanged at 15% and 13% respectively.

task1.title: Underground railway systems in five cities
task1.prompt: The table below gives information about the underground railway systems in five cities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

modelAnswer.text:
The table compares the underground railway networks of five cities in terms of when they opened, the length of their routes and the number of passengers they carry annually.

Overall, the older systems tend to be the most extensive, although the size of a network does not necessarily determine how heavily it is used. Tokyo's system is by far the busiest, while the Kyoto metro is the smallest by a wide margin.

London has the oldest underground railway, which opened in 1863, and it also has the longest route, at 402 kilometres. Paris followed in 1900 and Tokyo in 1927, with networks of 226 and 304 kilometres respectively. The two most recent systems, in Washington DC (1976) and Kyoto (1981), differ greatly in scale: Washington's route covers 208 kilometres, whereas Kyoto's is just 31 kilometres long.

In terms of passenger numbers, Tokyo carries an impressive 2,860 million people a year, almost twice as many as Paris (1,498 million). Despite having the longest network, London transports around 1,026 million passengers. Washington DC, meanwhile, serves only 112 million, fewer even than the much shorter Kyoto system, with 126 million.

task1.title: Recycling glass bottles
task1.prompt: The diagram below shows how glass bottles are recycled. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

steps: Used bottles are placed in public bottle banks
Bottles are collected by lorry and taken to a recycling plant
Glass is sorted by colour and washed to remove labels and dirt
Clean glass is crushed into small pieces called cullet
Cullet is mixed with sand, soda ash and limestone
The mixture is melted in a furnace at about 1,500°C
Molten glass is poured into moulds to form new bottles
New bottles are filled, sealed and delivered to shops

modelAnswer.text:
The diagram illustrates the stages by which used glass bottles are collected, processed and turned into new bottles that are returned to the shops.

Overall, the process is cyclical and consists of eight main steps, beginning with the collection of empty bottles from bottle banks and ending with the delivery of new, filled bottles to retailers.

At the first stage, consumers place their empty bottles in public bottle banks. These are then emptied by lorries, which transport the glass to a recycling plant. On arrival, the bottles are sorted according to colour and washed thoroughly so that labels and dirt are removed. The clean glass is subsequently crushed into small fragments, which are known as cullet.

In the next phase, the cullet is combined with raw materials, namely sand, soda ash and limestone. This mixture is heated in a furnace to a temperature of approximately 1,500 degrees Celsius until it melts. The molten glass is then poured into moulds, where it is shaped into new bottles. Finally, these bottles are filled with drinks, sealed and distributed to shops, after which the cycle can begin again.

modelAnswer.text:
The bar chart compares student numbers on five types of course at a technical college in 2014 and 2024, while the pie chart shows how students financed their studies in 2024.

Overall, enrolment shifted markedly towards computing and health care over the decade, while the more traditional practical subjects lost students. In terms of funding, government loans were the most common source of payment.

In 2014, engineering was the most popular course, with 820 students, followed by construction with 700. Health care, computing and hospitality attracted between 450 and 610 students each. Turning to funding, almost half of all students (46%) relied on a government loan in 2024. Employers paid the fees of nearly a quarter of learners (24%), and a further 18% were supported by their families. Only a small minority were funded by scholarships (8%) or paid from their own savings (4%).

task2.title: Working from home
task2.prompt:
Some people believe that working from home benefits both employees and employers. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Employers can recruit talent from any location
Lower office costs can be reinvested in staff
Employees save time and money on commuting
Flexible schedules can raise job satisfaction and loyalty
against: Staff may feel isolated and lonely
Junior employees lose informal learning from colleagues
Boundaries between work and home life can blur
Team creativity and spontaneous collaboration may suffer

modelAnswer.text:
Over the past decade, remote work has shifted from a rare privilege to a mainstream arrangement for millions of office staff. In my view, its advantages for both employers and employees clearly outweigh the drawbacks, provided that it is managed sensibly.

To begin with, companies can recruit talent regardless of location, which widens the pool of skilled applicants considerably. Moreover, savings on office space can be reinvested in training, technology or higher salaries. A firm that no longer rents an entire floor in a central business district, for instance, may be able to fund professional courses for every member of staff.

Employees, meanwhile, gain hours that would otherwise be lost to commuting. In congested cities such as Dhaka, where a single journey can exceed an hour, this time can be devoted to rest, exercise or family, all of which tend to improve concentration and job satisfaction. As a result, workers who are trusted to manage their own schedules are often more loyal and less likely to resign.

Admittedly, working from home is not without its challenges. Some staff feel isolated, and junior employees may miss the informal learning that happens in a shared office. However, these problems can largely be solved through regular video meetings and occasional in-person days rather than by abandoning remote work altogether. Indeed, many organisations already combine home and office working with considerable success.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that working from home benefits both sides of the employment relationship. With clear communication and a flexible hybrid model, its drawbacks are minor compared with the gains in productivity, cost and wellbeing.

task2.title: Practical skills at school
task2.prompt:
Some people believe that schools should teach practical life skills, such as managing money and cooking, instead of focusing mainly on academic subjects. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Young adults often lack basic budgeting skills and fall into debt
Cooking lessons can improve diet and long-term health
Not every family can teach these skills at home
Practical lessons engage students who struggle with theory
against: Academic knowledge is essential for further study and careers
Timetables are already overcrowded
Parents are responsible for teaching everyday skills
Literacy and numeracy underpin all practical skills anyway

modelAnswer.text:
It is sometimes argued that schools devote too much time to traditional academic subjects and too little to the practical skills that young people need in adult life. While I accept that such skills are valuable, I disagree that they should replace academic learning; instead, they should be integrated into it.

On the one hand, there is a strong case for teaching practical competences. Many young adults leave school without knowing how to create a budget, compare loans or cook a simple, nutritious meal. As a result, some fall into debt soon after receiving their first salary, while others rely heavily on processed food. Moreover, not every child grows up in a household where these lessons are passed on, so the school may be the only place where disadvantaged pupils can acquire them.

On the other hand, academic subjects provide the foundation for almost everything else. A student cannot understand interest rates without mathematics, nor read a rental contract carefully without strong literacy. Furthermore, subjects such as science and history develop analytical thinking, which is essential for higher education and for many careers. If these were reduced significantly, school leavers might be able to cook but would be poorly equipped to compete in a knowledge-based economy.

In my view, the most sensible solution is to combine the two. Mathematics lessons, for instance, could include projects on household budgeting, and science classes could explore nutrition through practical cookery. In this way, pupils would apply theoretical knowledge to real situations without sacrificing academic depth.

In conclusion, although practical life skills deserve a place in the curriculum, they should complement rather than replace academic subjects. A well-designed timetable can prepare young people both for further study and for independent adult life.

task2.title: Online shopping
task2.prompt:
More and more people are choosing to buy goods online rather than in shops. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Convenience: shop at any time from anywhere
Easy to compare prices and read reviews
Access to a far wider range of products
Helpful for elderly, disabled or rural consumers
against: Closure of high-street shops and loss of local jobs
Extra packaging and delivery emissions
Risk of fraud and data theft
Cannot see, touch or try products before buying

modelAnswer.text:
In recent years, a growing number of consumers have switched from visiting shops to purchasing goods on the internet. Although this development has certain drawbacks, I believe that its benefits are considerably greater.

The most obvious advantage of online shopping is convenience. Customers can order almost anything at any time of day, without travelling or queuing, which is particularly valuable for people with long working hours. In addition, the internet makes it easy to compare prices across dozens of retailers and to read reviews from previous buyers, so consumers are better informed and less likely to be overcharged. Online stores are also a lifeline for elderly or disabled people and for those in rural areas, who may otherwise have very limited access to shops.

Nevertheless, the trend does have negative consequences. Traditional high streets have suffered as footfall declines, and many small businesses have closed, taking local jobs with them. Furthermore, the rise in home deliveries has increased traffic and packaging waste. There is also the risk of online fraud, as criminals can steal card details from poorly protected websites.

However, I would argue that these problems can be addressed. Many independent retailers now sell online as well as in person, reaching customers far beyond their own town. Delivery firms are gradually adopting electric vans and recyclable packaging, and secure payment systems have made fraud much less common than it once was. The advantages, by contrast, are fundamental and lasting.

In conclusion, while online shopping has contributed to the decline of some high streets and has environmental costs, its convenience, choice and accessibility mean that the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

task2.title: Plastic in the oceans
task2.prompt:
Large amounts of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Cause: heavy use of single-use packaging
Cause: poor waste collection in many coastal regions
Cause: litter carried by rivers to the sea
Cause: lost fishing nets and equipment
against: Solution: taxes or bans on single-use plastics
Solution: invest in waste management in developing regions
Solution: deposit-return schemes for bottles
Solution: require manufacturers to fund recycling

modelAnswer.text:
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic find their way into the sea, harming marine life and entering the human food chain. This essay will examine the main causes of this problem and suggest some practical solutions.

The primary cause is the enormous quantity of single-use plastic that modern societies consume. Bottles, bags, straws and food packaging are designed to be used once and thrown away, and because they are cheap, there is little incentive to reuse them. A second cause is inadequate waste management. In many rapidly growing coastal cities, rubbish collection is irregular, and waste is often dumped in open sites or rivers, from which it is carried directly into the ocean. Finally, the fishing industry itself contributes, since lost or abandoned nets account for a significant proportion of plastic at sea.

Several measures could reduce this pollution. Governments should impose taxes on, or ban, the most common single-use items. The charge on plastic bags introduced in many countries, for example, has cut their use dramatically within a few years. Secondly, wealthier nations and international organisations could fund better waste collection and recycling facilities in regions where rubbish currently escapes into waterways. In addition, deposit-return schemes, in which customers receive a small refund for returning bottles, have proved highly effective at increasing recycling rates. Manufacturers could also be made legally responsible for the waste their products create.

In conclusion, ocean plastic results largely from excessive disposable packaging, weak waste systems and fishing practices. A combination of taxation, investment in infrastructure and producer responsibility offers the best chance of reducing the flow of plastic into the sea.

task2.title: Taxing sugary food
task2.prompt:
Some people think governments should tax sugary foods and drinks to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Higher prices reduce consumption, especially among young people
Manufacturers reformulate products with less sugar
Revenue can fund sport and health education
Lower rates of obesity and diabetes reduce healthcare costs
against: Hits low-income families hardest
Restricts personal freedom of choice
People may switch to other unhealthy products
Education may change habits more effectively than tax

modelAnswer.text:
Rising rates of obesity and diabetes have led some people to call for taxes on products that are high in sugar. I largely agree with this proposal, although I believe that a tax alone would not be sufficient to change people's eating habits.

The main argument in favour of such a tax is that price strongly influences behaviour. When sugary drinks become more expensive, people, and particularly teenagers with limited pocket money, tend to buy fewer of them. Perhaps more importantly, a tax encourages manufacturers to reformulate their products. In several countries that introduced a levy on soft drinks, companies reduced the sugar content of many popular brands in order to avoid the charge, which benefited every consumer without anyone having to change their shopping. In addition, the revenue raised can be used for health education or school sports facilities.

Critics argue that such taxes are unfair because they affect low-income households most, as these families spend a larger share of their income on food. Others claim that adults should be free to decide what they eat without government interference. These objections have some validity, but the burden of diet-related illness also falls heavily on poorer communities, and the cost of treating it is paid by all taxpayers. Moreover, people remain free to buy sugary products; they simply pay a price closer to their true social cost.

Nevertheless, taxation should form part of a wider strategy. Clear food labelling, cookery lessons in schools and restrictions on junk-food advertising to children would all reinforce its effect.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should tax sugary foods and drinks, as this is an effective way to reduce consumption and improve recipes, provided it is combined with education and other supporting measures.

In many countries, an increasing number of young people want to work for themselves rather than for a company. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Reason: digital platforms make starting a business cheaper
Reason: desire for independence and flexibility
Positive: encourages innovation and job creation
Positive: builds initiative and practical skills
against: Reason: lack of secure graduate jobs
Negative: irregular income and no sick pay or pension
Negative: many start-ups fail within a few years
Negative: isolation and long working hours

modelAnswer.text:
In many parts of the world, young people are increasingly choosing to become self-employed rather than join established companies. This essay will explain the reasons for this trend and argue that, on balance, it is a positive development.

There are several reasons why self-employment appeals to the younger generation. Firstly, technology has made it far easier and cheaper to start a business. With a laptop and a social media account, a graphic designer or a baker can reach customers across the country without renting premises. Secondly, many young people value independence and flexibility more highly than their parents did, and they are attracted by the idea of choosing their own projects and working hours. Finally, in some countries, secure entry-level jobs have become scarce, so creating their own work may seem the most realistic option.

In my opinion, this trend is largely beneficial. Young entrepreneurs often bring fresh ideas to the market, and successful small businesses eventually create jobs for others. Even those whose ventures do not succeed usually gain valuable skills, such as marketing, budgeting and negotiation, which make them more attractive to future employers. For the economy as a whole, a culture of initiative and innovation is a considerable asset.

That said, self-employment carries real risks. Income can be irregular, and freelancers typically have no paid holidays, sick pay or employer pension contributions. Governments could reduce these dangers by offering simple pension schemes and basic business training for new entrepreneurs.

In conclusion, the growth of self-employment among young people is driven by technology, changing values and a difficult job market. Provided that suitable support is available, I believe it is a positive development for individuals and society alike.

task2.title: Living alone
task2.prompt:
In many countries, more and more people are choosing to live alone. What are the reasons for this? Do you think it is a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Reason: people marry later or not at all
Reason: greater financial independence, especially among women
Positive: privacy and personal freedom
Positive: develops independence and self-reliance
against: Reason: longer life expectancy leaves many elderly people widowed
Negative: loneliness and mental health problems
Negative: higher housing demand and costs
Negative: less efficient use of energy and space

modelAnswer.text:
The number of single-person households has risen sharply in many countries over recent decades. In this essay, I will explore why this has happened and explain why I consider it a mixed, but mainly negative, development.

One key reason is that people are marrying later, or choosing not to marry at all, so there is a longer period of adulthood spent outside a family home. Rising incomes, particularly among women, have also made it financially possible for many adults to rent or buy a home of their own. In addition, because people now live longer, many elderly people continue to live alone after the death of a partner, often for twenty years or more.

Living alone certainly offers some benefits. It gives people complete privacy and control over their own space, and it can encourage independence and self-reliance. For young professionals, a period of living alone may be an important stage of personal development.

However, I believe the disadvantages are more serious. The most significant is loneliness, which research has linked to depression and poorer physical health, especially among older people who may go days without speaking to anyone. Furthermore, when each person occupies a separate flat, cities need far more housing, which pushes up prices and increases energy consumption, since heating and appliances are shared by fewer people. In already crowded cities such as London or Seoul, this places heavy pressure on the housing market.

In conclusion, the trend towards living alone results from later marriage, greater financial independence and longer lives. Although it brings freedom and privacy, its social and environmental costs lead me to view it as a largely negative development that governments and communities should take steps to address.

task2.title: Youth crime
task2.prompt:
In some countries, the number of crimes committed by teenagers is increasing. What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Cause: lack of parental supervision
Cause: poverty and limited opportunities
Cause: peer pressure and gang culture
Cause: school exclusion and boredom
against: Solution: youth centres, sport and mentoring programmes
Solution: support for struggling families
Solution: keep at-risk pupils in education
Solution: restorative justice rather than prison for first offences

modelAnswer.text:
In a number of countries, crime committed by teenagers appears to be on the rise, causing concern among parents and policymakers alike. This essay will discuss the main causes of this problem and propose several possible solutions.

The first cause is often found within the family. When parents work long hours or are absent altogether, teenagers may receive little supervision or guidance, and they are more likely to spend unstructured time on the streets. A second factor is poverty. Young people growing up in deprived neighbourhoods may see few legitimate routes to success, and some are tempted by the quick money offered by theft or drug dealing. Peer pressure also plays an important role, since adolescents are strongly influenced by the need to belong, and joining a group that breaks the law can seem attractive to those who feel excluded at school.

To tackle these causes, a combination of measures is required. Local authorities should invest in youth centres, sports clubs and mentoring schemes that offer young people a safe place to go and positive adult role models. Schools, meanwhile, should try to keep struggling pupils in education by providing extra support rather than excluding them, as exclusion frequently leads directly to crime. In addition, social services could offer practical help to families under strain. Finally, for first-time offenders, restorative justice, in which young people meet their victims and repair the harm they have caused, has been shown to reduce reoffending more effectively than detention.

In conclusion, youth crime is closely linked to weak supervision, poverty and peer influence. By providing constructive activities, educational support and more rehabilitative forms of justice, society can prevent many teenagers from following a criminal path.

task2.title: Negative news
task2.prompt:
News media tend to focus mainly on problems and negative events rather than positive developments. Some people think this is harmful to individuals and society. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Constant bad news can raise anxiety and hopelessness
Gives a distorted, overly pessimistic view of the world
May reduce trust in institutions and each other
Positive stories could inspire people to act
against: Journalism's role is to expose problems and hold power to account
Warning people about risks keeps them safe
Audiences choose to read dramatic stories
Positive news can seem like propaganda or advertising

modelAnswer.text:
It is often observed that newspapers, television and news websites concentrate heavily on disasters, crime and conflict while largely ignoring positive events. I partly agree that this has harmful effects, but I also believe that reporting problems is an essential function of the media.

There is little doubt that an unbalanced diet of bad news can damage individuals. People who follow the news closely may develop a sense of anxiety and helplessness, particularly when stories about war or climate change appear hour after hour on their phones. Moreover, constant negativity can distort people's understanding of the world. Many surveys have found that the public believes crime and poverty are increasing even in periods when they are actually falling, largely because dramatic incidents receive so much coverage. Such pessimism can undermine trust in institutions and discourage people from taking part in public life.

On the other hand, journalists are not simply entertainers. One of their most important duties is to expose corruption, injustice and danger so that governments and companies can be held accountable. A report on unsafe buildings or contaminated water may be deeply unpleasant, but it can save lives. If the media focused mainly on good news, they would risk becoming a kind of public relations service for the powerful.

The solution, in my opinion, is not to abandon negative reporting but to balance it. So-called constructive journalism, which explains what is being done to solve a problem as well as describing the problem itself, can inform audiences without leaving them feeling powerless.

In conclusion, although the media's focus on negative events can cause anxiety and a distorted view of reality, reporting problems remains vital. A more balanced approach would serve both individuals and society better.

task2.title: Multinational companies
task2.prompt:
Large multinational companies are opening branches and factories in many developing countries. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Creates jobs and raises wages
Transfers technology and management skills
Brings investment and tax revenue
Improves infrastructure and access to goods
against: Local businesses may be driven out
Profits flow back to wealthy countries
Risk of poor working conditions and pollution
Loss of cultural identity and local traditions

modelAnswer.text:
Over the past few decades, multinational corporations have established offices and factories in a large number of developing nations. While this trend raises legitimate concerns, I believe that its advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages.

The most important benefit is employment. A single factory run by an international firm can provide thousands of jobs, often at wages higher than those offered by local employers. Bangladesh's garment industry and Vietnam's electronics sector, for example, have lifted millions of people out of poverty in this way. In addition, multinationals bring technology and management expertise that gradually spread to local companies, as employees gain skills and later start their own businesses. Governments also benefit from tax revenue and from improvements to roads, ports and power supplies that such investment often requires.

However, the presence of global companies is not without problems. Small local firms may be unable to compete with the prices and marketing power of international brands, and some are forced to close. Furthermore, a large share of the profits is transferred to shareholders in wealthier countries rather than reinvested locally. There have also been serious cases of unsafe working conditions and environmental damage where regulation is weak.

Nevertheless, most of these drawbacks can be reduced through sensible policy rather than by rejecting foreign investment. Developing countries can enforce labour and environmental standards, require companies to source some materials locally and invest tax revenue in education, so that their own businesses become more competitive over time.

In conclusion, although multinational companies can harm local businesses and exploit weak regulation, the jobs, skills and investment they bring are substantial. With effective government oversight, I believe the advantages of their expansion clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

task2.title: Spending on space exploration
task2.prompt:
Some people think that governments should stop spending money on space exploration and use it to solve problems on Earth instead. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

for: Poverty, hunger and healthcare need urgent funding
Climate change requires massive investment
Private companies can now fund space projects
Public money should meet citizens' immediate needs
against: Space research produces useful technologies (satellites, materials)
Satellites monitor climate and disasters
Space budgets are small compared with total spending
Exploration inspires young people to study science

modelAnswer.text:
Some argue that the vast sums spent on space programmes would be better used to tackle poverty, disease and climate change here on Earth. Although I understand this view, I disagree that governments should abandon space exploration altogether.

Those who support the proposal make a reasonable point. Millions of people still lack clean water, adequate healthcare or enough to eat, and it may seem morally difficult to justify sending rockets to Mars while these needs remain unmet. Furthermore, private companies are now willing to invest in rockets and satellites themselves, so it could be argued that taxpayers no longer need to fund this work.

However, I believe this argument overlooks several important points. Firstly, space research has produced technologies that directly improve life on Earth. Satellite systems provide weather forecasts, navigation and communications, and they allow scientists to monitor deforestation, melting ice caps and rising sea levels with great accuracy. Without them, our response to climate change and natural disasters would be far less effective. Secondly, the budgets involved are relatively modest. In most countries with space programmes, spending on space represents less than one per cent of the government budget, so cancelling it would do little to solve global poverty. Finally, space exploration inspires young people to study science and engineering, fields on which future solutions to earthly problems will depend.

It is also questionable whether private firms, which are driven by profit, should control research that affects all of humanity.

In conclusion, while problems on Earth must remain a priority, space exploration contributes to solving many of them and costs comparatively little. Governments should therefore continue to fund it, alongside, rather than instead of, their efforts to improve life on our own planet.
